chapters.relation: Tom Gunning argues that pre-WWI 'actuality' film is a distinct form from Griersonian 'documentary,' governed by what he calls the 'view' aesthetic: films (phantom rides, travelogs, 'process films' like D'ou Viennent les Faux Cheveux or A Day in the Life of an English Coal Miner) that mime the act of looking and display rather than embedding images in an argument. He locates the shift to documentary in WWI propaganda films such as Londen in Oorlogstijd, where images become evidence within a discursive claim. The essay is film historiography rather than an application of a named philosopher, so no taxonomy slug fits its core argument.

Scott MacDonald contrasts Disney's True-Life Adventures (The Vanishing Prairie, The Living Desert), which anthropomorphize animals into 1950s middle-class nuclear families and naturalize Manifest Destiny, with Jean Painleve's science films (The Seahorse, Acera, The Vampire), which choose organisms precisely because their sexual and reproductive lives defy conventional human morality. Using Nichols's claim that nature film lacks documentary's 'voice,' MacDonald argues nature films always carry ideology, and that Microcosmos and the anti-anthropocentric attention to insects show the genre's untapped philosophical value against the humanities/sciences split dramatized in Su Friedrich's The Head of a Pin.

William Rothman reads Jean Rouch's ten-minute single-take The Drums of Yore: Tourou and Bitti (and the later Dogon films Funeral at Bongo and Ambara Dama) to argue that Rouch's 'cine-trance' and 'one take/one sequence' method fuse anthropology, philosophy and poetry, so that the camera's mere presence provokes the Songhay dancer's possession by the god Kure. Leaning wholly on Stanley Cavell's ontology of film (the world on film as 'skin of the world,' the photograph's object as its subject), Rothman claims filming itself possesses Rouch, revealing the invisible in the visible. Its governing philosopher, Cavell, is absent from the taxonomy.

William Day argues that Herzog's Cave of Forgotten Dreams, filming the 32,000-year-old Chauvet Cave paintings in 3D, works not by preserving a past but by transfiguring the present, placing the viewer in a 'mythological relation to time.' He reads three literary precursors to this cinematic 'doubleness'—Emerson's 'History' and 'The American Scholar' (the past made 'now'), Thoreau's spectator-self in Walden's 'Solitude,' and Weil's 'renunciation of time'—as antecedents to Cavell's ontology of film. The Fred Astaire shadow-dance from Swing Time, spliced into the cave footage, becomes Day's emblem of what becomes of things on film: the shadows dance on after Astaire stops.

Pederson and Zimmermann analyze Vincent Grenier's 'avant-doc' videos (Color Study: Slaterville New York, Watercolor: Fall Creek, Les Chaises, Armoire) as interventions in the philosophy of documentary landscape. They read his flattened tableau shots and digitally manipulated color fields against the Hudson River School and Ansel Adams's transcendentalist (Emersonian/Thoreauvian) American sublime, invoking Timothy Murray's Heideggerian poiesis of habitats and Baudrillard's simulation/simulacra to argue Grenier replaces representation of nature with simulation—e.g., the pigeon reacting to its mirror image in Armoire—dissolving the divide between the natural and the technological.

Ariella Azoulay reflects on her film Civil Alliances—Palestine 1947–48, built from Haganah-archive documents of over a hundred civil agreements between Jews and Arabs (such as the Deir Yassin/Givat Shaul good-neighbor pact) that historians erased to sustain a narrative of enduring national conflict. Filming twenty-five Arabs and Jews reciting these promises around a reconstructed 1947 map, she argues that 'sovereign citizenship' is a colonial historiographic tool and that these archival promises are not about the past but a renewable civil future. The argument is political and archival rather than an application of a taxonomy philosopher.

Diana Allan traces a single 1948 photograph of the Palestinian fisherman Said Otruk—the basis of her video portrait Still Life—to examine the tension between the evidentiary and the affective in documentary photographs. Drawing on Dewey's Art as Experience distinction between 'perception' that is fresh and alive and 'recognition' arrested for another purpose, plus Bazin, Barthes's punctum, Berger and Cavell, she argues that when seeing is subordinated to political/national purpose the image's resolution is reduced, and that her own misremembering of the photo mirrors Said's, revealing memory's mediated, refracted temporality.

Mieke Bal frames her documentaries Mille et un jours and the installation Nothing is Missing around the ethical tension between 'modesty' and 'intimacy' in filming trauma. She reads Descartes's Passions of the Soul against the vulgate dualist cogito—arguing the isolating 'I think, I am' enacts his own abandonment trauma—and sets it beside Spinoza's socially constituted subject, while using Berkeley's 'esse est percipi' (reversed via the empowering close-up of a mother's face) and Deleuze's affection-image and rhizome. The multiplied, dispersed 'voice' of the Tunisian wedding film and Elena's silences become tools of a 'migratory aesthetics.'

Bernadette Wegenstein examines her own cinema-verite practice in The Good Breast (and See You Soon Again), arguing that verite 'provokes' rather than merely produces truth through the filmmaker's participatory presence. She grounds this in Italian neorealism via Bazin (the real 'aimed at,' not re-presented) and Deleuze's Cinema II 'time-image'—a Bergsonian cinema 'of the seer' attuned to lived duration. Through her breast-cancer patient-characters (Doris, Carol, Debra, Shelia) and the surgeon Dr. Schnaper's trip to Saint Agatha's Catania, she shows how editing calls forth an 'alternate reality' and an existential (Kracauerian) realism.

holes.name: Stanley Cavell
holes.what: American philosopher of ordinary language, aesthetics and the ontology of film (The World Viewed), who held that film is 'a moving image of skepticism' presenting 'a world past.'
holes.why: Rothman's entire reading of Rouch's cine-trance rests on Cavell's ontology of film (the 'skin of the world,' the photographic object as subject), and Cavell is also the governing philosopher of chapters 12 and 15, yet no taxonomy slug names him.
